title: Gabor-Granger pricing method: how to run it and how it compares to Van Westendorp
summary: Gabor Granger shows where demand drops, not why. Learn how to run it, compare it to Van Westendorp, and capture the reasoning.
body_markdown:
What is a good sample size for a Gabor-Granger study? +


Vendor guidance sets a planning floor of at least 100 completes per segment analyzed separately, with more needed when customer segments will be compared against each other. Conveo also flags results below 30 valid participants with a caution.


What is the difference between Gabor-Granger and Van Westendorp? +


Gabor-Granger estimates demand and revenue at specific price points. Van Westendorp identifies an acceptable price range from four perception questions and, in its standard version, gives no demand or revenue estimate. Many teams run Van Westendorp first, then Gabor-Granger inside the range it finds.


How is Gabor-Granger different from conjoint analysis? +


As a survey-based pricing technique, Gabor-Granger tests one product in isolation across different price points, with no competitive context, while \[conjoint analysis\](/glossary/conjoint-analysis) tests multiple attributes, including pricing options, simultaneously. The Gabor-Granger model is faster to field but answers a narrower question.


How many price points should a Gabor-Granger study include? +


Many guides use around five price points: \[SurveyMonkey's guide\](https://www.surveymonkey.com/learn/product-development/gabor-granger/) uses a five-point price ladder, and \[Qualtrics\](https://www.qualtrics.com/support/common-use-case/xm-solutions/pricing-study-gabor-granger/) requires at least four. Space them evenly, anchor them on current pricing, the main competitor's price, and the cost floor, and set the highest price point above where you expect demand to fall.


Do Gabor-Granger pricing studies work across multiple markets? +


Yes, with localized price stimuli built from local currency, price endings, and reference prices rather than prices converted at a flat exchange rate. Identical wording, routing, and randomization across markets isolate genuine market differences from conversion artifacts.
